title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot
story:
In the great war at Kurukshetra between the five Pandava brothers and their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, no duel had ever mattered like this one. Arjuna, the Pandavas' finest bowman, and Karna, the champion of the Kaurava host, had met at last — and everything, both armies knew, hung on the outcome. Arjuna fought from a chariot driven by Krishna, his cousin and friend.

The fight had begun with Arjuna's weapon careering through the sky like lightning, swelling with power and consuming the Kaurava ranks, until the broken divisions of their army drew back to watch. Then Karna crushed it with showers of gold-winged shafts, using the great foe-killing weapon he had won long ago from Rama of the axe, and turned the fight back. Bending his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, he sent shaft after shaft that pierced Arjuna again and again.

So the two closed with each other, and the sky went dark. They struck like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons, and the sun itself disappeared beneath the downpour of arrows, until the whole sky was one vast web of shafts with no space between. The men watching from both armies could see nothing but arrows, and no one could tell where the next one would come from. Masters of every weapon, the two wove every manoeuvre they knew, each watching for the other's single lapse — the one opening that would end it.

Now Karna pressed his rival back, now Arjuna drove him in turn. The beings gathered in the sky shouted first "Excellent, O Karna!" and then "Excellent, O Arjuna!" while the earth sank deep beneath the weight of chariots and the trampling of horses and elephants. It was a passage of arms so dreadful that the other warriors on the field could only stand and wonder.

And in that darkness of arrows, something else was waiting for its opening too. The snake Aswasena had long been Arjuna's enemy, and he had hidden himself in the net of arrows above the field, biding his time. Now he let himself be fitted to a shaft, and Karna, bending his great bow, loosed him straight at Arjuna's head.

The shaft blazed as it flew through the sky, alive and burning, aimed to end the duel at a single stroke.

Krishna saw it coming — the way a man who has driven a thousand chariots sees the one arrow among ten thousand that matters.

With great speed and the greatest ease, he pressed the chariot down with his feet. The great car sank about a cubit into the earth — as deep as a man's forearm — and the white horses, white as the rays of the moon, bent their knees and laid themselves down on the ground.

The burning arrow passed low over Arjuna's head, close enough to graze it — and swept away only his diadem.

The crown fell to the earth, and the man who had worn it was still standing. The diadem was the mark by which the whole field knew Arjuna, and Karna's deadliest shaft had torn it from his head and left the head itself untouched. It had met a charioteer who would sink the very ground beneath his friend to keep that head upon his shoulders. In the middle of the greatest battle the world had ever seen, the moment that saved Arjuna came down to a man setting his feet a cubit deeper into the earth.

The chariot rose again, the moon-white horses came back to their feet, and the duel went on — but the opening had passed, and it had passed because of the man holding the reins. Krishna had raised no weapon that day. He had not needed one.
reflection: The episode makes Krishna's loyalty literal: he is not fighting, not speaking, only driving, and yet the whole outcome turns on his feet pressing a chariot into the earth. The divine protection here is not a weapon or a miracle of light but a quick, precise act of a charioteer who will not let his friend be taken.
content_note: Battle violence; an arrow narrowly misses Arjuna.
next_story_tease: But the duel between Karna and Arjuna was not yet decided.
hero_scene: Krishna, reins in hand, presses the chariot down into the earth with his feet as the white horses kneel, while Karna's blazing snake-arrow sweeps just over Arjuna's bowed head and knocks the diadem from his hair.
